title: Google Will Restrict Free and AI Plus Users to Fewer Gemini Models From October 9
excerpt: Free users lose Flash and Pro access; AI Plus loses Pro. But AI Pro subscribers at $19.99/month gain Deep Think reasoning — previously locked behind $99.99 Ultra plans.
body:
• From October 9, free Gemini app users will be limited to the Flash-Lite model — losing access to Flash (3.6) and Pro (3.1), according to Google's updated support documentation.
  • Google AI Plus subscribers ($4.99/month) will lose access to Pro, keeping Flash-Lite and Flash; Google says affected users will receive an email explaining exactly when the change hits their account.
  • AI Pro ($19.99/month) customers gain Deep Think, the "maximum parallel reasoning" mode previously reserved for $99.99/month Ultra plans — no model access is being taken from Pro or Ultra tiers.
  • In October, Google also plans "low," "medium" and "high" effort levels for each model: more thorough answers at the cost of more usage quota.

Google is redrawing the boundaries of what its Gemini app users get for free. Starting October 9, users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the lightest model in the lineup — Gemini Flash-Lite — while subscribers on the entry-level paid tier will lose access to the Pro model, according to an updated support document reported by 9to5Google.

What changes on October 9

The new access matrix, as reported from Google's documentation, is stark. Users without a plan: Flash-Lite only. Google AI Plus subscribers, who pay $4.99 a month: Flash-Lite and Flash, but no Pro. AI Pro ($19.99/month) and AI Ultra ($99.99/month and above): all three models, plus Deep Think.

Free accounts lose access to 3.6 Flash and 3.1 Pro once the cutoff hits, the publication reports. For Plus subscribers, the timing is personal: Google says each account will "receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect," so the cutoff date may not be identical for everyone.

Context: the second squeeze this year

The change follows a compute-based usage overhaul Google introduced in May, and it arrives days after the company unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, its most powerful model yet — first offered to AI Ultra subscribers. Google has yet to say where Argon fits in the new matrix: whether it will count as a Pro model or form an entirely new tier above it, according to 9to5Google.

The broader industry pattern is unmistakable. As AI models grow more capable and more expensive to serve, the free tier is becoming a deliberately narrower on-ramp: good enough to try, thin enough to push heavy users toward a subscription. OpenAI has been making similar moves with ChatGPT's own tiers, and Google's restructuring puts its lineup in direct parallel.

The sweetener for AI Pro

There is one genuine upgrade in the shuffle. AI Pro subscribers at $19.99 a month will gain Deep Think, the "maximum parallel reasoning" option that had previously been exclusive to the $99.99 and $199.99 Ultra plans — effectively a price cut of more than 80 percent for access to Google's most intensive reasoning mode. Separately, the new low/medium/high effort levels, expected later in October, mirror controls already available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity: dial up the effort for harder problems, at the cost of more of your usage limit.

What it means for users

Practically, the change divides Gemini users into two clear groups. Casual users who ask for summaries, rewrites and everyday answers will likely notice little difference on Flash-Lite. But anyone using the free app for coding help, deep research or complex reasoning will hit the wall quickly — those are exactly the workloads the Pro model and higher effort levels exist for. If you are on AI Plus for the Pro model, your decision simplifies: either the $4.99 tier still earns its keep for Flash and storage perks, or the move to AI Pro just became harder to resist.

What's next

Watch the Plus notification emails for individual cutoff dates, and watch where Gemini 4 Argon lands — if Google classifies it above Pro, even Pro subscribers may find the top of the ladder moved. The effort-level controls, due later in October, will be the first chance to see whether Google prices "thinking harder" by the task or by the subscription.
